message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; for specific situations you may want to consult an attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What the law says | Practical Tips | |------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlords may charge up to one month’s rent for a furnished unit and two months for an unfurnished unit.
• The deposit must be returned within 30 days after you move out, minus any lawful deductions (e.g., unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear).
• Landlords must provide a written itemized statement of deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease, move‑in inspection report, and any receipts for repairs.
• Request a written receipt for the deposit. | | **Habitability** | • Texas law requires landlords to keep the premises in a habitable condition (e.g., plumbing, heating, structural safety).
• If the landlord fails to maintain habitability, you may withhold rent, repair and deduct, or terminate the lease. | • Document problems with photos and written notices.
• Give the landlord a reasonable time to fix issues before taking action. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are reasonable. | • Pay on time or negotiate a payment plan if you’re having trouble. | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party may terminate a month‑to‑month lease with 30 days’ written notice.
• For fixed‑term leases, the landlord must give notice of non‑renewal at least 30 days before the lease ends. | • Keep a copy of any notice you receive. | | **Right to Privacy** | • Landlords must give reasonable notice (usually 24 hours) before entering the unit, except in emergencies. | • Ask for a written notice of entry and keep a log of visits. | | **Discrimination** | • Under the Texas Fair Housing Act, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or handicap. | • Report any discriminatory practices to the Texas Commission on Human Rights. | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major defect, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from your rent, provided you follow the proper procedure (written notice, reasonable time to repair, etc.). | • Keep receipts and document the defect. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlords must follow the Texas eviction procedure (notice, court filing, judgment).
• Common grounds: non‑payment of rent, lease violations, or unlawful activity. | • Respond promptly to notices; consider mediation or legal counsel. | | **Rent Control** | • Texas has no statewide rent‑control laws. | • Be aware that rent increases are generally at the landlord’s discretion, but must be in writing. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities. | • Verify utility responsibilities before signing. | | **Subletting** | • Subletting is allowed if the lease permits it or if the landlord consents. | • Get written consent and keep a copy. | | **Landlord’s Right to Inspect** | • Landlords may inspect the unit for maintenance or to show it to prospective tenants, but must give notice. | • Keep a log of inspections. | | **Tenant’s Right to Repair** | • If the landlord fails to fix a major problem, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from rent, but you must follow the proper procedure. | • Document the problem and the repair. | | **Legal Resources** | • Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA) provides tenant‑rights guides.
• Local tenant‑rights groups and legal aid clinics can help. | • Contact TDHCA or a local tenant‑rights organization for assistance. | ### Quick Checklist Before Signing a Lease 1. **Read the lease thoroughly** – note rent amount, due date, security deposit limits, pet policy, maintenance responsibilities, and notice requirements. 2. **Ask for a written itemized list of any existing damages** – this protects you from being charged for pre‑existing issues. 3. **Confirm the landlord’s contact information** – you’ll need it for notices and repairs. 4. **Verify that the lease complies with Texas law** – e.g., no illegal clauses, no excessive late fees. ### When Problems Arise - **Document everything** (photos, written notices, receipts). - **Communicate in writing** (email or certified mail) so you have a record. - **Give the landlord a reasonable time** to fix issues before withholding rent or terminating the lease. - **Seek mediation or legal advice** if the landlord does not comply. --- **Disclaimer:** This information is for general educational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice. For specific legal questions or disputes, consult a licensed attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.
